title: The Goose-Girl
paragraphs: A king who ruled a great country died, leaving his queen alone with their only child, a daughter of rare beauty. Her mother loved her dearly and treated her with great tenderness. There was also a kindly fairy who was fond of the princess and helped the queen look after her. When the girl was grown, she was promised in marriage to a prince who lived far away, and as the wedding day came close, she prepared to travel to his country. The queen, her mother, packed a great many costly things: jewels, gold and silver, ornaments, fine gowns, and in short everything a royal bride ought to have. She also sent along a waiting-maid, who was to ride with the princess and hand her over to the bridegroom, and each of them had a horse for the journey. The princess’s horse was a gift from the fairy. Its name was Falada, and it could speak.

When the time came to leave, the fairy went to her bedroom, took a little knife and cut a lock of her own hair. She gave it to the princess and said, “Keep this safe, dear child, because it is a charm, and it may help you on the road.” Then everyone said a sad goodbye to the princess. She tucked the lock of hair inside her dress, climbed onto her horse and rode off toward her bridegroom’s kingdom.

One day they were riding beside a brook, and the princess grew very thirsty. She said to her maid, “Please get down and bring me some water from that brook in my golden cup, because I want a drink.” “No,” said the maid. “If you’re thirsty, get down yourself, bend down to the water and drink. I’m not going to be your servant any longer.” The princess was so thirsty that she climbed down and knelt over the little brook to drink. She was afraid, and did not dare to take out her golden cup. She wept and said, “Alas, what will become of me?” And the lock of hair answered her:

“Alas, alas, if your mother knew,
Bitterly, bitterly she would rue.”
But the princess was gentle and meek, so she said nothing about her maid’s bad behavior and simply got back on her horse.

They rode on for a good while, until the day turned so hot and the sun so fierce that the bride grew thirsty again. At last they came to a river, and, forgetting how rudely her maid had spoken before, she said, “Please get down and bring me some water in my golden cup.” But the maid answered even more arrogantly than before: “Drink if you want to, but I won’t be your servant.” The princess was so thirsty that she got off her horse, lay down and bent her head over the flowing water. She cried and said, “What will become of me?” And the lock of hair answered her once more:

“Alas, alas, if your mother knew,
Bitterly, bitterly she would rue.”

As she leaned down to drink, the lock of hair slipped out of her dress and floated off on the water. She was too frightened to notice, but the maid saw it and was delighted, because she knew about the charm. She could see that, with the hair gone, the poor bride would be in her power. So when the bride had finished drinking and was about to mount Falada again, the maid said, “I’ll ride Falada now, and you can have my horse.” The princess had to give up her horse, and soon after that she was made to take off her royal clothes and put on her maid’s shabby ones.

Finally, as they came near the end of the journey, the treacherous servant threatened to kill her mistress if she ever told anyone what had happened. But Falada had seen everything, and he took careful note of it.

Then the maid mounted Falada, the real bride took the other horse, and they rode on like that until they reached the royal court. Their arrival was greeted with great joy. The prince rushed out to meet them and lifted the maid down from her horse, believing she was the one he was to marry. She was led upstairs to the royal chamber, while the true princess was told to wait down in the courtyard.

It happened that the old king had nothing to do just then, so he sat at his kitchen window, watching what went on outside, and he noticed her standing in the courtyard. She was pretty, and far too delicate-looking for a waiting-maid, so he went up to the royal chamber and asked the bride who the girl was that she had brought with her and left standing below. “I brought her along to keep me company on the road,” said the bride. “Please give the girl some work, so she isn’t idle.” For a while the old king could think of no work for her, but finally he said, “I have a boy who looks after my geese. She can go and help him.” The boy’s name, the one the real bride was to help with the king’s geese, was Curdken.

Soon afterward the false bride said to the prince, “Dear husband, please do me a favor.” “Gladly,” said the prince. “Then have one of your butchers cut off the head of the horse I rode here, because it was wild and gave me a great deal of trouble on the road.” The truth was that she was terrified Falada might one day speak and tell everything she had done to the princess. She got her way, and faithful Falada was killed. When the true princess heard of it, she wept, and she begged the man to nail Falada’s head up on a large dark gate of the city, which she had to pass through every morning and evening, so that she could still see him now and then. The butcher said he would do as she asked, and he cut off the head and nailed it up beneath the dark gate.
At dawn, when she and Curdken passed through the gate, she spoke sorrowfully:
“Falada, Falada, there you hang!”
and the head answered:

“Bride, bride, there you go!
Alas, alas, if your mother knew,
Bitterly, bitterly she would rue.”

Then they went out of the city and drove the geese along. When she reached the meadow she sat down on a grassy bank and let down her wavy hair, which was pure silver. Curdken saw it glittering in the sun and ran over, wanting to pull out a few strands, but she cried:

“Blow, breezes, blow!
Let Curdken’s hat go!
Blow, breezes, blow!
Let him after it go!
Over hills, dales and rocks,
Away may it whirl,
Till my silver locks
Are all combed and curled!”

A wind came up, so strong that it blew Curdken’s hat right off, and away it flew over the hills. He had to turn and run after it, and by the time he got back she had finished combing and curling her hair and had pinned it up safely again. He was angry and sulky and would not say a word to her. They watched the geese until it grew dark in the evening, and then drove them home.
On the following morning, when they came to the dark gate again, the poor girl glanced up at Falada’s head and called out:
“Falada, Falada, there you hang!”
and the head answered:

“Bride, bride, there you go!
Alas, alas, if your mother knew,
Bitterly, bitterly she would rue.”
Then she drove the geese on, sat down in the meadow again and began to comb out her hair as before. Curdken ran up and tried to grab it, but she called out quickly:

“Blow, breezes, blow!
Let Curdken’s hat go!
Blow, breezes, blow!
Let him after it go!
Over hills, dales and rocks,
Away may it whirl,
Till my silver locks
Are all combed and curled!”

Then the wind came and blew his hat off, and it flew a long way, over the hills and far away, so that he had to run after it. When he came back, she had tied up her hair again, and everything was safe. So they watched the geese until dark.

That evening, after they got home, Curdken went to the old king and said, “I don’t want that strange girl helping me with the geese any more.” “Why not?” asked the king. “Because she does no good at all. She just teases me all day long.” The king made him explain what had happened, and Curdken said, “When we go through the dark gate in the morning with our flock of geese, she cries out and talks to the head of a horse that hangs on the wall. She says:
“Falada, Falada, there you hang!”
and the head answers:

“Bride, bride, there you go!
Alas, alas, if your mother knew,
Bitterly, bitterly she would rue.”

And Curdken went on to tell the king what happened in the meadow where the geese grazed: how his hat was blown away, and how he had to run after it and leave his flock to look after itself. But the old king told the boy to go out again the next day. When morning came, the king stood hidden behind the dark gate and heard how she spoke to Falada and how Falada answered. Then he went out to the field and hid in a bush at the edge of the meadow. Before long he saw with his own eyes how they drove the geese along and how, after a little while, she let down her hair, glittering in the sun. And then he heard her say:

“Blow, breezes, blow!
Let Curdken’s hat go!
Blow, breezes, blow!
Let him after it go!
Over hills, dales and rocks,
Away may it whirl,
Till my silver locks
Are all combed and curled!”

Straight away a gust of wind came and carried off Curdken’s hat, and Curdken ran after it, while the girl went on combing and curling her hair. The old king saw all of this. He went home without being seen, and when the little goose-girl came back in the evening, he called her aside and asked why she did these things. But she burst into tears and said, “I must not tell you, or any man, or I will lose my life.”

But the old king begged and pleaded so hard that she had no peace until she had told him the whole tale, from beginning to end, word for word. It was lucky for her that she did, because when she finished, the king had royal clothes put on her and stared at her in wonder, she was so beautiful. Then he called his son and told him that he had only a false bride, a mere waiting-maid, while the true bride was standing right there. The young king was overjoyed when he saw her beauty and heard how meek and patient she had been. Without a word to the false bride, the king ordered a great feast to be prepared for the whole court. The bridegroom sat at the head of the table, with the false princess on one side and the true one on the other. Nobody recognized her, because her beauty dazzled their eyes, and in her brilliant dress she looked nothing like the little goose-girl.

When they had eaten and drunk and were in high spirits, the old king said he would tell them a story. He began, and told the whole tale of the princess as though he had heard it somewhere long ago. Then he asked the true princess’s waiting-maid what she thought should be done to anyone who behaved like that. “Nothing better,” said the false bride, “than to put her in a barrel studded with sharp nails, harness two white horses to it, and have them drag it from street to street until she is dead.” “You are the one!” said the old king. “You have passed judgment on yourself, and so it shall be done to you.” Then the young king married his true wife, and they ruled the kingdom in peace and happiness for the rest of their lives. The good fairy came to visit them, and she brought faithful Falada back to life.
